lead: An open thin wall — an angle, tee, Z or channel — resists torque mainly by twisting each strip about its own centre line: St Venant torsion. Stiffness grows with the cube of wall thickness, so a 2 mm stiffener is very soft compared with a closed box. This chapter gives J = (1/3)Σbt³, surface shear stress and twist, and explains why a torsion box is a closed cell with open stringers riveted on.
prereq: You need Chapter 5.4 for the closed-box comparison and Unit 4 for the torque–twist relation.

sections.h3: Open walls twist strip by strip

blocks.text: An open section has no closed loop. A torque T (N·mm) cannot set up shear flow round a circuit, because none exists. Each strip twists about its mid-line. This is St Venant torsion.

Inside a strip shear stress is zero at mid-thickness and rises linearly to maxima at both surfaces. Those surface stresses form a couple over the thickness t, a short lever arm, so torsional stiffness is small.

blocks.where: J is the torsional constant (mm⁴); b is one wall length along its centre line (mm); t is that wall thickness (mm); the sum covers every wall.

blocks.text: The cube dominates. Doubling every t raises J eight times; halving t cuts J to one eighth. Adding width b helps only in proportion, so long thin walls are poor torsion members.

Open sections warp: angle legs sweep axially in opposite directions. The formula assumes free warping. A rib or fixed end restrains it, adds axial stress and stiffens the member; that is restrained torsion, not covered here.

sections.h3: Surface stress and rate of twist

blocks.where: τ<sub>max</sub> is surface shear stress (N/mm²); T is torque (N·mm); t<sub>max</sub> is the thickest wall (mm); J is the torsional constant (mm⁴). At distance n from mid-thickness, τ = T n / J.

θ is total twist over length L (radians); L is length (mm); G is shear modulus (N/mm²), about 27 000 for aluminium and 79 000 for steel; J is the torsional constant (mm⁴). Twist per unit length is θ/L = T/(GJ) rad/mm.

items: τmax occurs in the thickest wall, not the thinnest. Stress is zero at mid-thickness, so a thick wall climbs further.
For an equal angle with legs b and thickness t, J = (2/3) b t³. Add flange and web separately for a tee. Open sections suit bending and buckling, not torsion.

sections.h3: A closed box versus the open angle

blocks.text: A 60 mm × 60 mm angle of 2 mm wall uses about 120 mm of strip along its centre line. Bend 232 mm of the same 2 mm strip into a square box with centre-line side 58 mm: the box uses about twice the strip. Its perimeter is s = 4 × 58 = 232 mm and enclosed area A = 58 × 58 = 3364 mm². Bredt–Batho theory (Chapter 5.4) gives J = 4A²t/s.

blocks.where: A is area enclosed by the wall centre line (mm²); t is wall thickness (mm); s is centre-line perimeter (mm).

blocks.text: Now the whole perimeter carries constant shear flow q = T/(2A). At T = 200 N·m, L = 2 m, G = 27 GPa, the table compares the angle with the box.

The box is about 1219 times stiffer and about 84 times less stressed at the same torque, but it uses about twice the strip. Per unit material the closed form is still far better. This is why a wing torsion box is a closed cell between spars; open stringers carry bending and delay buckling (Unit 6). If an open section must carry torque, close it with a plate or rib.

figure.caption: Shear stress through the wall thickness at T = 200 N·m: zero at mid-thickness and 1250 MPa at both surfaces of the open angle, while a closed box using about twice the strip carries the same torque at a flat 14.9 MPa.

spec.aria: A V-shaped line rising from zero at mid-thickness to 1250 MPa at each surface of an open wall, with a flat line at 14.9 MPa for the closed box.

examples.question: A 60 mm × 60 mm × 2 mm equal angle, 2 m long, aluminium with G = 27 GPa, carries T = 200 N·m. (a) Find J, maximum shear stress and total twist. (b) A 232 mm length of the same strip is formed into a closed square box with centre-line side 58 mm (about twice the angle's strip). Find J and twist at the same torque, and compare.
steps: Angle: each centre-line leg b = 60 mm, t = 2 mm. Σbt³ = 60 × 2³ + 60 × 2³ = 960 mm⁴.
This exceeds aluminium yield (roughly 300–450 N/mm²), so the elastic answer is hypothetical.
Compare: J ratio = 390 224/320 = 1219. Box stress τ = T/(2At) = 200 000/(2 × 3364 × 2) = 14.9 N/mm². Box uses about twice the strip.
examples.answer: Open angle: J = 320 mm⁴, τ<sub>max</sub> = 1250 N/mm², θ = 46.3 rad (2653°). Box: J = 390 224 mm⁴, θ = 0.0380 rad (2.18°), τ = 14.9 N/mm². At equal torque it is about 1219 times stiffer, with about twice the strip.
examples.check:
import math
b, t, L, G, T = 60.0, 2.0, 2000.0, 27000.0, 200000.0
J_open = (1/3)*(b*t**3 + b*t**3)
print('J_open =', round(J_open, 2))
tau_open = T*t/J_open
print('tau_open =', round(tau_open, 2))
theta_open = T*L/(G*J_open)
print('theta_open_rad =', round(theta_open, 4))
print('theta_open_deg =', round(math.degrees(theta_open), 1))
A = 58.0*58.0
s = 232.0
J_closed = 4*A**2*t/s
print('J_closed =', round(J_closed, 1))
theta_closed = T*L/(G*J_closed)
print('theta_closed_rad =', round(theta_closed, 5))
print('theta_closed_deg =', round(math.degrees(theta_closed), 2))
print('ratio =', round(J_closed/J_open, 1))
q = T/(2*A)
print('tau_closed =', round(q/t, 2))

traps: Feeding an open section to Bredt. For this angle the 60 mm × 60 mm outline gives 390 224 mm⁴ instead of 320 mm⁴ — wrong by about 1220.
Writing Σbt instead of Σbt³. The cube is the physics; the linear sum is a different quantity with different units.
Measuring b at the outer face, or counting a corner twice. Take b along the wall centre line; the error is small for 2 mm walls but visible at 4 mm.
Reporting τ<sub>max</sub> at mid-thickness or on the thinnest wall. It is zero at mid-thickness and largest on the thickest wall.

Unit slips: convert torque to N·mm (×1000) and G to N/mm² (×1000). Leaving G in GPa makes θ 1000 times too large (46 296 rad instead of 46.3 rad); leaving T in N·m makes it 1000 times too small (0.0463 rad = 46.3 mrad). Make both slips and the errors cancel, so the answer looks right in the wrong units. Always convert first.

quiz.q: Write J for a thin-walled open section and define each symbol with its unit.
quiz.a: J = (1/3) Σbt³, where b is wall length along its centre line (mm), t is wall thickness (mm), and J is in mm⁴. Sum over every wall.

quiz.q: How does shear stress vary through the wall thickness of an open section under torque?
quiz.a: It is zero at mid-thickness and rises linearly to equal and opposite maxima at both surfaces.

quiz.q: Why does an open wall resist torque so poorly compared with a closed tube?
quiz.a: The resisting couple inside a strip acts over t, a short lever arm, so stiffness scales as t³. In a closed tube shear flow runs round the full perimeter at large distance from the axis, and J depends on enclosed area squared.

quiz.q: A flat strip 100 mm wide and 3 mm thick, 1 m long, carries T = 50 N·m with G = 27 GPa. Find J, τ<sub>max</sub> and twist.
The wall thickness of an open section is tripled everywhere. How do J, τ<sub>max</sub> and twist change at the same torque?
quiz.a: J rises 27 times. τ<sub>max</sub> = Tt/J changes by 3/27 = 1/9, so falls to one ninth. Twist falls to 1/27.

quiz.q: A 200 mm length of the same 3 mm strip (twice the material of Q4) is closed into a square box with mean side 50 mm. Compare its twist with the open strip of Q4 at the same torque.
quiz.a: Q4 strip: J = 900 mm⁴. Box: A = 50 × 50 = 2500 mm², s = 200 mm, J = 4 × 2500² × 3/200 = 375 000 mm⁴, ratio 375 000/900 = 417. Twist at equal torque falls from 2.06 rad to 0.00494 rad. The gain is at equal torque, not equal material; the box uses twice the material.

quiz.q: What is warping of an open section, and when do the simple torsion formulas stop being accurate?
quiz.a: Cross sections do not stay plane: points at leg tips move axially in opposite directions. The formulas assume free warping; a rib or fixed end restrains it, axial stresses appear and the member stiffens.

quiz.q: Why does a wing torsion box use a closed cell for torque while its stringers are open sections?
quiz.a: The closed cell has J proportional to A²t/s, so a thin skin gives high stiffness, low stress and small twist. Open stringers have J proportional to bt³ and would twist too much, so they carry bending and delay skin buckling, not torque.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real open-section members are restrained at ribs and fittings, so free-warping formulas over-predict twist. Vlasov theory adds a warping constant and a slower-decaying stress system; finite element codes use warping degrees of freedom. Search for non-uniform torsion of open thin-walled sections and warping constant C<sub>w</sub>.
